description: Urchin was a web statistics analysis program developed by Urchin Software Corporation. It analyzed web server log file content and displayed the traffic information on that website based upon the log data.

name: Slide
description: Slide was a photo sharing software for social networking services such as MySpace and Facebook. Later Slide began to make applications and became the largest developer of third-party applications for Facebook.

name: Google Friend Connect
description: Google Friend Connect was a free social networking site from 2008 to 2012.

name: Jaiku
description: Jaiku was a social networking, micro-blogging and lifestreaming service comparable to Twitter.

name: Google Code Search
description: Google Code Search was a free beta product which allowed users to search for open-source code on the Internet.

name: Google Health
description: Google Health was a personal health information centralization service that provided users a merged health record from multiple sources.

name: Smart Personal Objects Technology (SPOT)
description: Smart Personal Objects Technology (SPOT) was a initiative to create intelligent and personal home appliances, consumer electronics, and other objects through new hardware capabilities and software features.

name: iTunes Ping
description: Apple's music-focused social network. Steve Jobs personally called Mark Zuckerberg to negotiate a Facebook tie-in. Zuckerberg asked for too much; Ping launched anyway and flopped.

name: MobileMe
description: Apple's cloud sync and email service. So unreliable at launch that Steve Jobs called it an embarrassment to the entire company at an internal meeting. Replaced by iCloud.

name: 30-pin Dock Connector
description: The wide 30-pin connector used on every iPod and iPhone for nine years. It spawned an entire accessories industry: alarm clocks, car adapters, speaker docks. Killed overnight by Lightning.

name: iChat
description: Apple's instant messaging client, supporting AIM, Jabber, and Bonjour. The colorful chat bubbles became iconic before iChat was rebranded as Messages and folded into iMessage in OS X Mountain Lion.

name: Safari for Windows
description: Apple's attempt to bring Safari to Windows, announced by Steve Jobs as part of his iPhone web strategy. It was quietly abandoned after Safari 5.1.7 in 2012, while Mac Safari continued on.

name: iWork.com
description: Apple's web-based document sharing and commenting service for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. It never escaped beta, then was shut down as Apple pushed users toward iCloud.

name: Chomp
description: An app search and discovery engine that helped users find apps by what they did, not just what they were called. Apple acquired it to improve App Store search, then shut the service off.

name: MacBook Pro (17-inch)
description: Apple's biggest professional notebook, beloved by editors, developers, and anyone who wanted a portable desktop. Killed when Retina MacBook Pros arrived and Apple decided 15 inches was enough.

name: Noop Programming Language
description: Noop was a project by Google engineers Alex Eagle and Christian Gruber aiming to develop a new programming language that attempted to blend the best features of 'old' and 'new' languages and best practices.

name: Apture
description: Apture was a service that allowed publishers and bloggers to link and incorporate multimedia into a dynamic layer above their pages.

name: Google Buzz
description: Google Buzz was a social networking, microblogging and messaging tool that integrated with Gmail.

name: Gears
description: Gears (aka Google Gears) was utility software that aimed to create more powerful web apps by adding offline storage and other additional features to web browsers.

name: Google Notebook
description: Google Notebook allowed users to save and organize clips of information while conducting research online.

name: ZygoteBody
description: ZygoteBody, formerly Google Body, was a web application by Zygote Media Group that rendered manipulable 3D anatomical models of the human body.

name: Zune Media Player
description: Zune was a line of portable media players.

name: Google PowerMeter
description: Google PowerMeter was a software project of Google's philanthropic arm that helped consumers track their home electricity usage.

name: Google Squared
description: Google Squared was an information extraction and relationship extraction product that compiled structured data into a spreadsheet-like format.

name: Google Sidewiki
description: Google Sidewiki was a browser sidebar tool that allowed users to contribute information to any web page.

name: Aardvark
description: Aardvark was a social search service that connected users live with friends or friends-of-friends who were able to answer their questions.

name: Google Pack
description: Google Pack was a collection of software tools offered by Google to download in a single archive. It was announced at the 2006 Consumer Electronics Show, on January 6. Google Pack was only available for Windows XP, Windows Vista, and Windows 7.

name: Google Desktop
description: Google Desktop allowed local searches of a user's emails, computer files, music, photos, chats and Web pages viewed.

name: Google Fast Flip
description: Google Fast Flip was an online news aggregator, something of a high tech microfiche.

name: Google Dictionary
description: Google Dictionary was a standalone online dictionary service.

name: Kin
description: Kin was a short-lived mobile phone line from Microsoft designed for users of social networking.

name: Google Labs
description: Google Labs was a technology playground used by Google to demonstrate and test new projects.

name: Google Rebang
description: Rebang was a Zeitgeist-like service centered on providing service to a Chinese audience. It was incorporated into Google Labs as of late 2010, and later discontinued along with its parent project.

name: Google Directory
description: Google Directory was an Internet website directory organized into 14 main categories that allowed users to explore the web.

name: Google Image Swirl
description: Google Image Swirl was an enhancement to the image search tool that came out of Google Labs. It was built on top of image search by grouping images with similar visual and semantic qualities.

name: Google Real-Time Search
description: Google Real-Time Search provided live search results from Twitter, Facebook, and news websites.

name: Google Script Converter
description: Google Script Converter was an online transliteration tool for transliteration (script conversion) between Hindi, Romanagari, and various other scripts. It's ended because Google shut down Google Labs and all associated projects.

name: Google Sets
description: Google Sets generates a list of items when users enter a few examples. For example, entering "Green, Purple, Red" emits the list "Green, Purple, Red, Blue, Black, White, Yellow, Orange, Brown".

name: Google Specialized Search
description: Google Specialized Search allowed users to search across a limited index of the web for specialized topics like Linux, Microsoft, and 'Uncle Sam.'

name: Google Hotpot
description: Google Hotpot was a local recommendation engine that allowed people to rate restaurants, hotels, etc. and share them with friends.

name: Gizmo5
description: Gizmo5 was a VOIP communications network and a proprietary freeware soft phone for that network.

name: Windows Embedded Automotive
description: Windows Embedded Automotive (formerly Microsoft Auto, Windows CE for Automotive, Windows Automotive, and Windows Mobile for Automotive) was an operating system subfamily of Windows Embedded based on Windows CE for use on computer systems in automobiles.

name: Windows Virtual PC
description: Windows Virtual PC (formerly Microsoft Virtual PC 2007, Microsoft Virtual PC 2004, and Connectix Virtual PC) was a virtualization program for Microsoft Windows originally developed as a Macintosh application for System 7.5 by Connectix.

name: Real Estate On Google Maps
description: Real Estate on Google Maps enabled users to find places for sale or rent in an area they were interested in.

name: fflick
description: fflick was a review, information, and news website that used information from aggregated Tweets to rate movies as positive or negative.

name: Microsoft Money
description: Microsoft Money was a personal finance management software program. It has capabilities for viewing bank account balances, creating budgets, and tracking expenses, among other features.

name: Windows Live Spaces
description: Windows Live Spaces (previously MSN Spaces) was a highly customizable blogging and social networking platform that integrated closely with MSN Messenger.

name: Final Cut Studio
description: Apple's flagship pro-video suite bundling Final Cut Pro, Motion, Soundtrack Pro, DVD Studio Pro, and later Color and Compressor. It dominated mid-2000s Mac video production until Final Cut Pro X blew up the old suite model.

name: Apple Cinema Display
description: Apple's widescreen external monitors, beloved by designers and video editors. The Cinema Display line was replaced by the Thunderbolt Display in 2011.

name: Final Cut Server
description: A collaborative media asset management system for Final Cut Pro workflows in studios and broadcast. Discontinued in 2011 during Apple's messy Final Cut Pro X transition.

name: Front Row
description: A full-screen media center app for Macs, designed to be controlled from the couch with the Apple Remote. Killed in OS X Lion without a replacement.

name: iDVD
description: DVD menu and disc authoring software bundled with every Mac. Made beautiful animated menus, until optical drives quietly disappeared from Apple hardware forever.

name: iWeb
description: Drag-and-drop personal website creator, tightly integrated with MobileMe hosting. As MobileMe was wound down and iCloud offered no web hosting replacement, iWeb was left behind.

name: Logic Express
description: The affordable entry point to professional music production on Mac. Killed when Apple slashed Logic Pro 9's price to $199, eliminating the need for a budget tier.

name: Rosetta
description: The translation layer that let PowerPC apps run on Intel Macs, enabling Apple's first major chip transition without breaking software. Removed in OS X Lion.

name: Xserve
description: Apple's rack-mounted 1U server hardware and one of Apple's few genuine enterprise products. Discontinued as Apple pushed customers toward Mac Pro and Mac mini server configurations.

name: iSync
description: A Mac utility for syncing contacts, calendars, and bookmarks across Macs, phones, and iPods over Bluetooth or USB. Removed from OS X Lion as iCloud made manual device sync feel obsolete.

name: Final Cut Express
description: Apple's semi-pro video editor for people who wanted more than iMovie but less than full Final Cut Pro. Discontinued during the Final Cut Pro X reset.

name: Soundtrack Pro
description: Apple's professional audio editing and sound design app for video editors. Bundled with Final Cut Studio, then killed when Apple collapsed the old pro video suite.

name: DVD Studio Pro
description: High-end DVD authoring software for creating professional menus, masters, and replicated discs. Essential in the DVD era, stranded when Apple decided optical media was over.

name: Color
description: A professional color-grading app born from Apple's acquisition of Silicon Color. It brought serious finishing tools to Final Cut Studio, then disappeared in the Final Cut Pro X transition.

name: Google Base
description: Google Base was a database provided by Google into which any user can add almost any type of content, such as text, images, and structured information.

name: Windows Live FrameIt
description: Windows Live FrameIt was a service under the Windows Live brand to extend the functionality of digital photo frames or any RSS enabled devices, allowing the users to customise the displayed information using multiple data sources.

name: GOOG-411
description: GOOG-411 (or Google Voice Local Search) was a telephone service that provided a speech-recognition-based business directory search.

name: Microsoft Amalga
description: Microsoft Amalga Hospital Information System (HIS), formerly Hospital 2000, was a fully integrated hospital information system designed for developing and emerging markets.

name: Windows Essential Business Server 2008
description: Windows Essential Business Server 2008 (code named Centro) was an operating system for server for mid-size businesses (up to a maximum of 300 Users and/or Devices).

name: Response Point
description: Response Point was an advanced VoIP-based telephone system targeting small businesses.

name: BumpTop
description: BumpTop was a skeuomorphic desktop environment app that simulates the normal behavior and physical properties of a real-world desk and enhances it with automatic tools to organize its contents.

name: Windows MultiPoint Mouse
description: Windows MultiPoint Mouse was a technology that enables the use of multiple pointing devices on the same computer.

name: Google SearchWiki
description: SearchWiki was a Google Search feature which allowed logged-in users to annotate and re-order search results.

name: YouTube Streams
description: YouTube Streams allowed users to watch a YouTube video together while chatting about the video in real-time.

name: Marratech e-meetings
description: Marratech was a Swedish company that made software for e-meetings (e.g., web conferencing, videoconferencing).

name: Windows Mobile
description: Windows Mobile was a family of mobile operating systems developed by Microsoft for smartphones and Pocket PCs.

name: Project Origami
description: Project Origami was the code name for ultra-mobile PCs (also known as ultra-mobile personal computers or UMPCs), a class of laptops whose specifications were defined in collaboration with Intel.

name: Visual FoxPro
description: Visual FoxPro was data-centric procedural programming language with object-oriented programming (OOP) features.

name: Lala.com
description: A cloud music service where users could stream their libraries and buy cheap web-only songs. Apple acquired it in 2009 and shut it down months later, years before Apple Music arrived.

name: Google Web APIs
description: The Google Web APIs were a free SOAP service for doing Google searches so that developers could use the results in almost any way they wanted.

name: Microsoft Office Accounting
description: Microsoft Office Accounting (formerly Small Business Accounting) was an accounting software application targeting small businesses that had between 1 and 25 employees.

name: Google Ride Finder
description: Google Ride Finder was a service that used GPS data to pinpoint and map the location of taxis, limos, and shuttle vehicles available for hire in 10 U.S. metro areas.

name: Microsoft Works
description: Microsoft Works was an intuitive and cheap alternative to Office. It included a word processor, a spreadsheet and a database management system. Later versions had a calendar application and a dictionary.

name: Google Toolbar for Firefox
description: Google Toolbar for Firefox

name: Microsoft AutoCollage
description: Microsoft AutoCollage (re-named in Microsoft Research AutoCollage and Microsoft Research AutoCollage Touch) was a photomontage desktop application to create a collage of representative elements from a set of images, able to detect and empathize faces and objects.

name: Soapbox on MSN Video
description: Soapbox on MSN Video was an internet video-sharing service offered via MSN portal, similar to YouTube.

name: Microsoft Popfly
description: Microsoft Popfly was a website that allowed users to create web pages, program snippets, and mashups using the Microsoft Silverlight rich web applications runtime.

name: Google Radio Automation
description: Google Radio Automation was a hardware and software service used by radio operators to automate song playing among other radio station functions.

name: On2 Flix Cloud
description: Flix Cloud was a high-capacity online video encoding service.

name: Google Mashup Editor
description: Google Mashup Editor was an online web mashup creation service with publishing, syntax highlighting, and debugging.

name: Windows Live OneCare
description: Windows Live OneCare (previously Windows OneCare Live) was a computer security and performance enhancement service developed for Windows based on multi-platform RAV (Reliable Anti-virus) technology.

name: MSN QnA
description: MSN QnA (formerly Live Search QnA and Windows Live QnA) was a question and answer service, part of MSN group of services where users could ask questions, tag them according to topic, and gain points and reputation for answering other users' questions.

name: Microsoft Content Management Server
description: Microsoft Content Management Server was a web-based content management system to prepare and publish web-based content, originally developed by NCompass Labs Inc. and finally acquired by Microsoft in 2001.

name: Google Shared Stuff
description: Google Shared Stuff was a web page sharing system that allowed users to bookmark pages and share them.

name: Grand Central
description: Grand Central was a Voice over IP service that was acquired by Google, and turned into Google Voice.

name: Dodgeball
description: Dodgeball was a location-based social network where users texted their location to the service, and it notified them of friends and points of interest nearby.

name: Google Audio Ads
description: Google Audio Ads service allowed advertisers to run campaigns on AM/FM radio stations in the US using the AdWords interface.

name: Encarta
description: Microsoft Encarta was a digital multimedia encyclopedia, originally sold on CD-ROM or DVD, then available on the internet via a subscription, and finally turned into free and supported by advertisements.

name: Tafiti
description: Tafiti was an animated search engine launched by Microsoft and TrappsInteractive to showcase the Silverlight animation and video player.

name: Ms. Dewey
description: Ms. Dewey was a web search engine based on an experimental interface, developed in Adobe Flash, for Live Search, where the eponymous Ms. Dewey, played by actress Janina Gavankar, acted as an interactive search assistant for the user's inquiries.

name: Shake
description: Professional VFX compositing software used on major Hollywood films. Apple acquired it, sold it as a high-end Mac tool, then discontinued it in 2009 without a direct successor.

name: Mighty Mouse
description: Apple's first widely sold multi-button mouse, with a tiny clickable scroll ball on top. The ball clogged easily, leaving users rolling it upside down on paper to bring it back to life.

name: Wireless Mighty Mouse
description: The cordless version of Apple's tiny-scroll-ball mouse, built for the pre-Magic Mouse era of AA batteries and Bluetooth desktops. It only lasted three years before Apple junked the scroll ball and switched to a touch surface.

name: AppleTalk
description: The networking protocol that let any Mac on a LocalTalk cable share files and printers with zero configuration. Phased out in macOS Snow Leopard after 24 years, as Apple standardized on TCP/IP and Bonjour.

name: Google Lively
description: Google Lively was a web-based virtual environment that provided a new way to access information.

name: SearchMash
description: SearchMash was an experimental, non-branded search engine that Google used to be able to play around with new search technologies, concepts, and interfaces.

name: Google Page Creator
description: Google Page Creator was a website creation and hosting service that allowed users to build basic websites with no HTML knowledge.

name: MSN Music
description: MSN Music was a store of music, music news, music videos, spotlights on new music, artist information, and live performances of artists.

name: Send to Phone
description: Google Send to Phone was an add-on to send links and other information from Firefox to their phone by text message.

name: Onfolio
description: Onfolio was an online research tool to collect data from the web and make annotations such as inking and text highlighting.

name: Windows Live Expo
description: Windows Live Expo was a classified advertisements website, similar to Craigslist, with sections devoted to different topics such as jobs, housing, gigs, and résumés.

name: Google Browser Sync
description: Google Browser Sync was a Firefox extension that synced information like passwords and browsing history.

name: Live Search Academic
description: Live Search Academic was a web search engine for scholarly literature that existed, part of Microsoft's Live Search services.

name: Hello
description: Hello was a service by Picasa that let users share pictures "like you're sitting side-by-side."

name: Outlook Express
description: Outlook Express, formerly known as Microsoft Internet Mail and News, was an email and news client included with Internet Explorer versions 3.0 through to 6.0.

name: Classic Visual Basic
description: Classic Visual Basic (formerly only Visual Basic) was a third-generation event-driven programming language known for its Component Object Model (COM) programming model.

name: Google Web Accelerator
description: Google Web Accelerator was a client-side software that increased the load speed of web pages.

name: Windows Messenger
description: Windows Messenger was an instant messaging client included in Windows XP and designed for both corporate and home users.

name: Microsoft Media Services
description: Windows Media Services (WMS) was a streaming media server software that allows a Windows Server administrator to generate streaming media (audio/video).

name: Xserve RAID
description: Apple's 3U rack-mount RAID array for Xserve and pro media workflows. It offered unusually cheap high-capacity storage for its day, then disappeared as Apple backed away from enterprise storage hardware.

name: .Mac
description: The paid successor to iTools: @mac.com email, iDisk cloud storage, and online sync for $99/year. Frequently unreliable. Rebranded as the even more unreliable MobileMe.

name: Zeitgeist
description: Google Zeitgeist was a weekly, monthly, and yearly snapshot in time of what people were searching for on Google all over the world.

name: NewsBot
description: NewsBot was a search engine specialized to offer personalized news using advanced MSN Search technology.

name: Google Click-to-Call
description: Google Click-to-Call allowed a user to speak directly over the phone to businesses found in search results.

name: Google Video Player
description: The Google Video Player plays back files in Google's own Google Video File (.gvi) media format and supported playlists in 'Google Video Pointer' (.gvp) format.

name: Google Video Marketplace
description: Google Video Marketplace was a service that included a store where videos could be bought and rented.

name: Microsoft Digital Image
description: Microsoft Digital Image (formerly Picture It!) was a photo editing application designed for casual users and initially inspired to the wizard user interface concepts of Microsoft Publisher.

name: Visual J#
description: Visual J# was a programming language and development tooling which was meant to help Java developers move to the .NET ecosystem.

name: Microsoft NetMeeting
description: Microsoft NetMeeting was VoIP and multi-point videoconferencing client and incorporated technology acquired from Data Connection Ltd and DataBeam Corporation.

name: DirectSound3D
description: DirectSound3D was an extension to DirectSound to standardize real-time 3D audio, allowing games to use a single API instead of coding for each sound card manufacturer.

name: Office Assistant
description: Office Assistant was an intelligent user interface for Microsoft Office that assisted users by way of an interactive animated character which interfaced with the Office help content. The most famous avatar was Clippit (a.k.a. Clippy), a humanized paperclip.

name: Microsoft Fingerprint Reader
description: Fingerprint Reader was an USB Fingerprint reader to unlock PC and apps.

name: AppleWorks
description: Apple's bundled office suite, born as ClarisWorks in 1991. For 16 years it was the word processor and spreadsheet for millions of Mac and Apple II users. Retired when iWork arrived.

name: Apple Pro Keyboard
description: Apple's full-size clear-plastic desktop keyboard with built-in USB ports, bundled across the early G4 era. It lasted until Apple went thinner, flatter, and aluminum with the 2007 Apple Keyboard.

name: iPod Hi-Fi
description: Apple's $349 boombox speaker dock for the iPod, personally championed by Steve Jobs at its launch as audiophile-quality. Discontinued 18 months later as the rest of the speaker industry caught up and sold the same thing for less.

name: Classic Environment
description: The compatibility layer that let Mac OS 9 apps run inside early Mac OS X. It kept old software alive through the transition, then disappeared in Mac OS X Leopard.

name: Google Answers
description: Google Answers was an online knowledge market.

name: Microsoft Office FrontPage
description: Microsoft Office FrontPage was a WYSIWYG HTML editor and website administration tool for Windows.

name: MSN Chat
description: MSN Chat was the Microsoft Network version of IRCX (Internet Relay Chat extensions), which replaced Microsoft Chat.

name: Writely
description: Writely was a Web-based word processor.

name: Google Public Service Search
description: Google Public Service Search provided governmental, non-profit and academic organizational search results without ads.

name: Google Deskbar
description: Google Deskbar was a small inset window on the Windows toolbar and allowed users to perform searches without leaving the desktop.

name: Microsoft Visual SourceSafe
description: Microsoft Visual SourceSafe (VSS) was a source control program oriented towards small software development projects, originally created by One Tree Software prior to Microsoft acquisition in 1994.

name: Microsoft Photo Story
description: Microsoft Photo Story was a free application that allows users to create a visual story (show and tell presentation) from their digital photos.

name: Apple Wireless Mouse
description: Apple's first Bluetooth mouse, launched alongside the first Apple Wireless Keyboard to cut cable clutter from Mac desks. It lasted until Apple replaced it with the more capable Wireless Mighty Mouse.

name: eMac
description: An education-focused all-in-one Mac built around a 17-inch CRT. Initially sold only to schools, briefly offered to consumers, then returned to education before being discontinued in 2006.

name: iSight
description: Apple's sleek external FireWire webcam: aluminum, cylindrical, and perfectly designed. Discontinued once Apple started building cameras into iMacs, MacBooks, and displays.

name: iMac G5
description: The flat-panel all-in-one that hid the whole computer behind the screen and paved the way for every modern iMac. It barely had time to settle in before Apple switched the line to Intel.

name: iBook
description: Apple's consumer laptop line, born as the colorful G3 clamshell in tangerine and blueberry and later refined into the white iBook. Retired when Apple switched to Intel and replaced it with the MacBook.

name: Power Mac G5
description: Apple's aluminum tower with a perforated cheese-grater face, promoted as the world's fastest personal computer. Steve Jobs promised 3GHz within a year. It never came, and Apple jumped to Intel two years later.

name: PowerBook
description: Apple's professional laptop line for 15 years, evolving from the chunky 100 series to the titanium and aluminum G4. Retired when Apple switched to Intel and rebranded the line as MacBook Pro.

name: Microsoft Plus!
description: Microsoft Plus! was a commercial enhancement for Windows which included a variety of software such as screensavers, themes, games, and multimedia applications.

name: iPod mini
description: The colorful, compact iPod that made portable music fashionable. It quickly became a hit, then was discontinued to make way for the even thinner iPod nano.

name: Soundtrack
description: Apple's loop-based royalty-free music tool for video editors, DVD authors, and web developers. It was later reinvented as the more ambitious Soundtrack Pro and disappeared as its own product.

name: Production Suite
description: Apple's short-lived pre-Final Cut Studio bundle, combining Final Cut Pro HD, Motion, and DVD Studio Pro into a single pro-video suite. It was a transitional product and lasted less than a year.

name: Apple Pro Mouse
description: Apple's first optical mouse, shipped in translucent clear plastic after the hockey puck debacle. Cleaner, saner, and still stubbornly one-button until Mighty Mouse finally gave Apple users scrolling and right-click.

name: Sherlock
description: The system search tool in Mac OS that hunted across local files, the web, and online databases. Replaced by Spotlight in 2005 and remembered as the origin of 'sherlocked', the verb for when Apple kills a third-party app by building its features in.

name: Microsoft PhotoDraw 2000
description: Microsoft PhotoDraw 2000 was a vector graphics and raster imaging software.

name: Microsoft bCentral
description: Microsoft bCentral was a service for small businesses to easily establish an online presence with integrated suite of services for site creation and hosting, web communications, and online marketing.

name: Microsoft Broadband Networking
description: Microsoft Broadband Networking was a series of computer networking hardware products ranging from Wi-Fi routers to network cards.

name: Visual J++
description: Visual J++ (pronounced "Jay Plus Plus") was a Microsoft's implementation of Java which ran only on MSJVM, the proprietary JVM.

name: HyperCard
description: A revolutionary hypermedia and scripting environment that predated and inspired the World Wide Web. Quietly abandoned, then left to wither for a decade before being killed entirely.

name: Apple Studio Display
description: Apple's CRT and flat-panel monitor line from the translucent late-90s and early-2000s era. It carried Apple from VGA and ADC into the LCD age, then disappeared when the company consolidated its displays around the aluminum DVI Cinema lineup.

name: Apple Display Connector
description: Apple's one-cable display connector that combined power, USB, and video for flat-panel Macs. Elegant and very Apple, but proprietary enough that it was swept away when Apple moved its displays to industry-standard DVI.

name: iMac G4
description: The sunflower iMac, with a flat-panel display floating on a chrome arm above a hemispherical dome. Beloved by designers and discontinued when Apple moved toward putting the whole computer behind the screen.

name: Microsoft Photo Editor
description: Microsoft Photo Editor was a raster graphics editor component of Microsoft Office first included with Microsoft Office 97 that provided editing tools to texturize, create negatives, adjust gamma, and add transparency to GIF images.

name: ILoo
description: iLoo was a smart portable toilet integrating the complete equipment to surf the Internet from inside and outside the cabinet.

name: Kakuto Chojin
description: Kakuto Chojin: Back Alley Brutal was a fighting game for the Xbox gaming console, retired after few months because its controversial content.

name: Cinema Tools
description: Apple's film-editing companion for Final Cut Pro, built for cut lists, change lists, and 24 fps workflows. It lasted barely a year as a standalone app before Apple folded it into Final Cut Pro 4.

name: AirPort Base Station (Dual Ethernet)
description: Apple's second-generation flying-saucer Wi-Fi base station, with built-in firewall, dual Ethernet ports, and AOL support. It vanished when Apple jumped to 802.11g and renamed the line AirPort Extreme.

name: AirPort Card
description: Apple's original 802.11b wireless card for the iBook and other AirPort-ready Macs. It helped drag Wi-Fi into the mainstream, then gave way to the smaller, faster AirPort Extreme Card with 802.11g.

name: iMac G3
description: The translucent Bondi Blue all-in-one that helped pull Apple back from the brink. Designed under Jony Ive, later offered in fruity colors, and proof that Apple could still ship something the world wanted.

name: Power Mac G4
description: Apple's pro tower line through the early Mac OS X years, spanning Graphite, Quicksilver, Mirrored Drive Doors, and the first mass-market dual-processor Macs. It defined the classic expandable Power Mac before the G5 made everything larger, louder, and 64-bit.

name: Microsoft Data Analyzer
description: Microsoft Data Analyzer was a program to analyze and visualize data and data trends, and was integrated with SQL Server Analysis Services.

name: Myth: The Fallen Lords
description: Myth: The Fallen Lords was a real-time tactics video game developed originally by Bungie until Microsoft bought and discontinued it to let the developers focus on Halo.

name: Active Server Pages (ASP)
description: Active Server Pages (ASP) was the Microsoft's first server-side scripting language and engine for dynamic web pages, and it was the predecessor of ASP.NET.

name: iTools
description: Apple's first internet services bundle, offering a free @mac.com email address and iDisk cloud storage. Replaced by the paid .Mac subscription service.

name: Macintosh Server G4
description: Apple's pre-Xserve tower server, essentially a Power Mac G4 sold with AppleShare IP or Mac OS X Server for schools and workgroups. It was Apple's last server before the company finally built a proper rackmount machine.

name: Mac OS 9
description: The final version of the classic Mac OS, foundation of Apple computing for 18 years. Steve Jobs literally held a funeral for it on stage at WWDC 2002, complete with eulogy, organ music, and an open coffin.

name: Microsoft BackOffice Server
description: Microsoft BackOffice Server was a computer software package featuring Windows NT Server and other Microsoft server products that ran on NT Server.

name: Microsoft Java Virtual Machine
description: Microsoft Java Virtual Machine (MSJVM) was a proprietary Java virtual machine.

name: AirPort Base Station (Graphite)
description: The original flying-saucer Wi-Fi base station Apple launched with the iBook, complete with a built-in 56K modem and 10BASE-T Ethernet. It helped kick-start mainstream Wi-Fi before Apple replaced it with a more capable second-generation model.

name: Power Mac G4 Cube
description: A fanless, silent 8-inch cube of a Mac and a genuine design triumph. But at $1,799, with limited expandability and cheaper Power Mac G4 towers nearby, it was a commercial failure.

name: Microsoft Vizact
description: Microsoft Vizact was a program that allowed creation of interactive documents using HTML+TIME (Timed Interactive Multimedia Extensions).

name: Microsoft Liquid Motion
description: Microsoft Liquid Motion was an application to create Java animations to compete with Macromedia Flash.

name: Digital Sound System 80
description: The Digital Sound System 80 (DSS80) was a three-piece PC audio system co-developed with Philips.

name: DriveSpace
description: DriveSpace (initially known as DoubleSpace) was an OS service to increase the amount of data the user could store on disks by transparently compressing and decompressing data on-the-fly.

name: QBasic
description: QBasic was an integrated development environment and interpreter for a variety of dialects of BASIC which are based on QuickBASIC.

name: ActiMates
description: ActiMates was a family of interactive stuffed toys which can interact with many episodes of their respective TV shows or on special ActiMates-compatible VHSes and special PC games.

name: Hockey Puck Mouse
description: The round USB mouse that shipped with the original iMac G3. Impossible to orient by feel and hated by every reviewer who touched it. Replaced within two years by the Apple Pro Mouse and remembered as a cautionary tale in industrial design.

name: Microsoft Comic Chat
description: Microsoft Comic Chat (later Microsoft Chat) was a graphical IRC client.

name: Microsoft Cordless Phone System
description: The Microsoft Cordless Phone System (also known as PC Phone System MP-900) was a cordless telephone featuring personal computer integration and it was the first Microsoft's first telephone of any kind.

name: Take Control TC1000
description: Harman/Kardon Take Control TC1000 was an IR remote control designed in conjunction with Microsoft equipped with a LCD touchscreen to control any device and customizable via a desktop application.

name: Power Macintosh G3
description: Apple's first G3 desktop line, spanning the beige minitowers and the later blue-and-white tower that dragged the pro Mac into the USB era. It briefly gave Apple a speed story again, then vanished when the G4 arrived with faster graphics and a louder marketing machine.

name: Newton MessagePad
description: Apple's pioneering PDA, famous for ambitious handwriting recognition that became a punchline. Steve Jobs canceled the Newton platform in 1998 after returning to Apple.

name: eMate 300
description: A Newton-powered clamshell laptop built for students, with an integrated keyboard and weeks of battery life. Killed alongside the Newton when Steve Jobs returned.

name: Microsoft Cinemania
description: Microsoft Cinemania was an application distributed on CD-ROMs that shown information about films such as images, sound clips, dialogues, sound tracks and some full motion video clips.

name: Creative Writer
description: Creative Writer was a word processor designed for children.

name: Microsoft GIF Animator
description: Microsoft GIF Animator was a computer software program to create simple animated GIFs.

name: Apple QuickTake
description: One of the first consumer digital cameras, made by Fujifilm and sold under Apple's name. Steve Jobs killed the entire product line within weeks of returning to Apple.

name: Pippin
description: Apple's multimedia gaming platform co-developed with Bandai. It sold only about 42,000 units worldwide and cost nearly $600 at launch. An ambitious experiment in all the wrong directions.

name: OpenDoc
description: Apple's ambitious component-based document framework, designed to replace monolithic apps with modular parts. Steve Jobs killed it soon after returning to Apple in 1997, calling it a distraction.

name: Cyberdog
description: Apple's OpenDoc-based internet suite with a web browser, email, news, FTP, and address book components. When OpenDoc was killed, Cyberdog was abandoned with it.

name: Apple Network Server
description: A short-lived PowerPC server line that did not even run Mac OS, shipping instead with IBM AIX. Expensive, strange, and canceled during Apple's 1997 product purge.

name: LaserWriter line
description: Apple's PostScript laser printer family, a key piece of the desktop publishing revolution. Once essential to the Mac ecosystem, it was killed when Steve Jobs cut non-core peripherals.

name: Microsoft Anti-Virus for Windows
description: Microsoft Anti-Virus (MSAV) was an antivirus program introduced for MS-DOS operating system, finally acquired and dismissed by Symantec.

name: Microsoft Bob
description: Microsoft Bob was a user-friendly interface for the Windows 3.1x, Windows 95 and Windows NT operating systems.

name: 3D Movie Maker
description: 3D Movie Maker (3DMM) was a children's computer program to make films by placing 3D characters and props into pre-rendered environments, as well as adding actions, sound effects, music, text, speech and special effects.

name: eWorld
description: Apple's cheerful AOL rival, built around a cartoon town of email, forums, news, and downloads. It was Mac-only, expensive, barely marketed, and shut down with only a fraction of AOL's audience.

name: A/UX
description: Apple's first official Unix operating system, blending UNIX System V with a familiar Macintosh interface. It gave Apple a credible enterprise Unix story years before Mac OS X, then vanished without a successor.

name: Macintosh TV
description: A Mac LC 520 in a black case with a built-in TV tuner, and Apple's first attempt at merging computing and television. Only 10,000 units were ever made and it was never sold outside the US.

name: Apple II line
description: The 8-bit computer family that made Apple a real company and dominated classrooms for years. It outlived the Apple III, Lisa, and many early Macs before Apple finally ended the line in 1993.

name: Xenix
description: Xenix was a version of the Unix operating system for various microcomputer platforms, licensed by Microsoft from AT&T Corporation in the late 1970s that reached the largest market share among Unix OSs in mid '80s.

name: Apple Lisa
description: Apple's first GUI-based business computer at $9,995. Technically remarkable, commercially ruinous, and quickly outclassed and outpriced by the Macintosh.

name: Apple III
description: Apple's business computer, plagued by overheating and reliability problems after Apple chose silence over a cooling fan. The redesigned Apple III Plus arrived too late to save the line.
